01: The Louisiana Purchase Exposition, the St. Louis World's Fair, closes in Forest Park after seven months and more than 19 million visitors.
02: Under the stands of Stagg Field at the University of Chicago, Enrico Fermi's team starts Chicago Pile-1: the first human-made self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction.
03: Engineer Neil Papworth sends the first text message, from a computer to a Vodafone phone in Britain. It reads 'Merry Christmas'.
04: The National Grange of the Order of Patrons of Husbandry is founded: the oldest national farm organization in the United States.
The brigantine Dei Gratia finds the Mary Celeste adrift and deserted between the Azores and Portugal. No one from her crew was ever found.
05: Flight 19, five Navy Avenger torpedo bombers from Fort Lauderdale, vanishes on a training flight. All 14 airmen are lost, and 13 more in a search plane.
06: The French cargo ship Mont-Blanc collides with the Imo in Halifax harbour and explodes, killing at least 1,782 people: the largest human-made explosion up to that time.
07: Japan attacks Pearl Harbor. All eight U.S. battleships present are damaged, four are sunk, and 2,403 Americans are killed.
Apollo 17 lifts off at 12:33 a.m. Eastern, the only night launch of a Saturn V and the last crewed flight to the Moon.
08: Eli Whitney is born in Westborough, Massachusetts. His cotton gin of 1793 reshaped the farm economy of the South.
Samuel Langley's Aerodrome collapses on launch and falls into the Potomac River for the second time. Nine days later the Wright brothers fly.
09: In San Francisco, Douglas Engelbart's 90-minute demonstration shows the computer mouse, windows, hypertext and video conferencing: 'the Mother of All Demos'.
10: Japanese bombers sink HMS Prince of Wales and HMS Repulse off Malaya, the first capital ships sunk solely by air power while steaming at sea.
11: Apollo 17's lunar module lands in the Taurus-Littrow valley: the most recent time people have set foot on the Moon.
12: On Signal Hill in Newfoundland, with an antenna held up by a kite, Marconi reports hearing the Morse letter S sent from Cornwall, about 2,200 miles away.
13: Francis Drake leaves Plymouth with five ships. He returned in September 1580, having sailed around the world.
14: Mariner 2 passes about 21,600 miles from Venus: the first spacecraft to successfully encounter another planet.
15: Gemini 6A, flown by Wally Schirra and Tom Stafford, closes to within one foot of Gemini 7: the first crewed rendezvous in space.
16: At 2:15 a.m. the first of the great New Madrid earthquakes strikes the Mississippi valley. The shaking was felt as far away as Canada, and the river briefly ran backward.
Germany launches its Ardennes offensive, the Battle of the Bulge: the largest and bloodiest single battle fought by the United States in World War II.
17: Near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, Orville Wright flies 120 feet in 12 seconds. Wilbur's fourth flight of the day covers 852 feet in 59 seconds.
The Douglas DST, prototype of the DC-3 airliner, makes its first flight, 32 years to the day after the Wright brothers.
18: Gaston de Chasseloup-Laubat sets the first recognized automobile land speed record at Acheres, France: 39.2 miles per hour in a Jeantaud electric car.
SCORE, the world's first purpose-built communications satellite, is launched. It relayed a recorded greeting from President Eisenhower from orbit.
19: The BBC Empire Service, today's World Service, begins shortwave broadcasts from Daventry, England.
20: France hands New Orleans to the United States under the Louisiana Purchase. St. Louis held its own transfer ceremony, Three Flags Day, in March 1804.
21: Apollo 8 launches with Borman, Lovell and Anders: the first crewed spacecraft to leave Earth's gravity and reach the Moon.
22: At Bastogne, Brig. Gen. Anthony McAuliffe answers a German demand to surrender with one word: 'NUTS!'
23: At Bell Labs, Walter Brattain demonstrates a working point-contact transistor to colleagues and managers: often given as the birth date of the transistor.
24: By his own account, Reginald Fessenden broadcasts music and a Bible reading from Brant Rock, Massachusetts, to ships at sea. Historians still argue whether it happened.
In orbit around the Moon, the Apollo 8 crew reads from Genesis on live television and photographs Earthrise.
25: The locomotive Best Friend of Charleston makes its inaugural run in South Carolina. Its railroad ran the first scheduled steam passenger trains in the United States.
26: A surprise blizzard finishes burying New York City: 26.4 inches of snow in Central Park, and 77 deaths across the Northeast.
27: HMS Beagle sails from Plymouth under Robert FitzRoy with the naturalist Charles Darwin aboard. The voyage lasted nearly five years.
28: Scotland's Tay Rail Bridge collapses in a gale as a passenger train crosses it. Everyone aboard is killed; 59 deaths were confirmed.
29: Thomas Edison is granted U.S. patent 465,971 for signaling without wires between elevated plates on masts: an early wireless telegraph.
30: The U.S. signs the Gadsden Purchase, paying Mexico $10 million for land in today's southern Arizona and New Mexico, wanted for a southern railroad to the Pacific.
31: The ironclad USS Monitor sinks in a storm off Cape Hatteras, North Carolina, while under tow. Sixteen of her crew are lost.
